Anycast.Description: AS uses anycast for at least one IP address.
Anycast.Background: Reimplements the intended semantics of BGP.tools's identically-named public tag using this toolkit's own feature snapshots, rather than reusing BGP.tools's logic directly -- BGP.tools does not publish its tagging methodology, so this is a transparent, documented reconstruction. See Chen, Bischof, Testart, and Dainotti, 'Rethinking and facilitating how we classify Autonomous Systems by network properties,' IMC 2026, Appendix G.2 (https://doi.org/10.1145/3777912.3839831).

Tranco 10k Host.Description: AS hosts domains in the Tranco top domains list.
Tranco 10k Host.Background: Reimplements the intended semantics of BGP.tools's identically-named public tag using this toolkit's own feature snapshots, rather than reusing BGP.tools's logic directly -- BGP.tools does not publish its tagging methodology, so this is a transparent, documented reconstruction. See Chen, Bischof, Testart, and Dainotti, 'Rethinking and facilitating how we classify Autonomous Systems by network properties,' IMC 2026, Appendix G.2 (https://doi.org/10.1145/3777912.3839831).

IPv6 Only.Description: AS originates IPv6 prefixes but no IPv4 prefixes.
IPv6 Only.Background: Reimplements the intended semantics of BGP.tools's identically-named public tag using this toolkit's own feature snapshots, rather than reusing BGP.tools's logic directly -- BGP.tools does not publish its tagging methodology, so this is a transparent, documented reconstruction. See Chen, Bischof, Testart, and Dainotti, 'Rethinking and facilitating how we classify Autonomous Systems by network properties,' IMC 2026, Appendix G.2 (https://doi.org/10.1145/3777912.3839831).

No Eyeball.Description: AS has no inferred eyeballs (end users).
No Eyeball.Background: A simple complement of eyeball presence, introduced in Appendix I of the AS Tagging paper (Chen, Bischof, Testart, and Dainotti, IMC 2026, https://doi.org/10.1145/3777912.3839831) so ASes can be tagged along the transit and residential-access dimensions independently, instead of forcing them into the small number of mutually exclusive AS-type categories (e.g. CAIDA AS Classification, PeeringDB Network Type) that Section 4 of the paper shows fail to separate ASes with similar feature combinations.

No Transit.Description: AS does not provide IP transit at all.
No Transit.Background: One of three transit-role tags (No Transit / Sibling Transit / Public Transit) introduced in Section 6 of the AS Tagging paper (Chen, Bischof, Testart, and Dainotti, IMC 2026, https://doi.org/10.1145/3777912.3839831). Motivation: existing practice infers transit status from CAIDA AS Classification's coarse Transit/Access category plus customer-AS information (e.g. Marcos, Prehn, Leal, Dainotti, Feldmann, and Barcellos, 'AS-Path Prepending: There Is No Rush Without a Push,' IMC 2020, https://doi.org/10.1145/3419394.3423642), which the paper argues misses many ASes that do provide transit. No Transit directly checks for the absence of any customer AS rather than relying on that coarse category.
No Transit.Logic: For a given AS, it does not have any ASes as customers.

Sibling Transit.Description: AS only carries traffic internally within its organization to its sibling ASes.
Sibling Transit.Background: One of three transit-role tags (No Transit / Sibling Transit / Public Transit) introduced in Section 6 of the AS Tagging paper (Chen, Bischof, Testart, and Dainotti, IMC 2026, https://doi.org/10.1145/3777912.3839831), to distinguish ASes that provide transit only within their own organization from those that sell it externally -- a distinction the paper argues coarse mutually-exclusive AS-type categories collapse. Example from the paper: AS20940 (Akamai) is the sole upstream provider for 15 sibling Akamai ASes, so all of its transit stays inside the organization.
Sibling Transit.Logic: For a given AS, all direct customer ASes are its sibling ASes. Computed directly from caida-asrel_customer_list + inetintel-as2org_sibling_list when the raw list is available; otherwise read from the precomputed caida-asrel_customer_all_sibling column (the published snapshot release does not include the raw list). None if neither is available.

Public Transit.Description: AS provides IP transit service to ASes owned by other downstream organizations.
Public Transit.Background: One of three transit-role tags (No Transit / Sibling Transit / Public Transit) introduced in Section 6 of the AS Tagging paper (Chen, Bischof, Testart, and Dainotti, IMC 2026, https://doi.org/10.1145/3777912.3839831), to identify ASes that sell IP transit to unrelated organizations. The paper reports that this tag identifies 3,854 transit ASes not captured by IPinfo's coarse ISP category, including data-center/colocation operators such as AS23686 (Equinix Connect) that IPinfo instead labels 'Hosting.'
Public Transit.Logic: For a given AS, some direct customer ASes are not its sibling ASes. Computed directly from caida-asrel_customer_list + inetintel-as2org_sibling_list when the raw list is available; otherwise read from the precomputed caida-asrel_customer_has_nonsibling column (the published snapshot release does not include the raw list). None if neither is available.

Country Code.Description: ISO country code where the AS number was registered (RIR delegation record). Administrative attribute; distinct from geolocation-based Any Presence / Domestic.
Country Code.Background: Covers the jurisdiction-based notion of AS "nationality" -- where an AS is registered, rather than where its infrastructure or address space is physically located -- used in research with emphasis on legal/regulatory jurisdiction. For example, Trusin, Bertholdo, and Santanna, 'The Effect of the Russian-Ukrainian Conflict from the Perspective of Internet eXchanges,' CNSM 2022 (https://doi.org/10.23919/CNSM55787.2022.9964765), used this definition to track how many Russian and Ukrainian ASes became unreachable during the conflict, and for how long. See Appendix H of the AS Tagging paper (Chen, Bischof, Testart, and Dainotti, IMC 2026, https://doi.org/10.1145/3777912.3839831).

Any Presence.Description: Returns list of country codes where AS has any IP presence (IPv4 or IPv6).
Any Presence.Background: Covers the geolocation-based definition of AS presence in a country -- any IP address geolocated there, regardless of concentration -- used in research on Internet shutdowns. For example, Padmanabhan, Filastò, Xynou, Raman, Middleton, Zhang, Madory, Roberts, and Dainotti, 'A Multi-Perspective View of Internet Censorship in Myanmar,' FOCI @ ACM SIGCOMM 2021 (https://doi.org/10.1145/3473604.3474562), defined the ASes "potentially impacted" by Myanmar's 2021 government-ordered Internet shutdown as those with any IP presence in the country, determined from IP geolocation data. See Appendix H of the AS Tagging paper (Chen, Bischof, Testart, and Dainotti, IMC 2026, https://doi.org/10.1145/3777912.3839831), which reproduces this definition as a composite tag.
Any Presence.Logic: Union of country codes from maxmind-geolite2_cc_v4_list and cc_v6_list.

Domestic.Description: Domestic AS. Defined by Gamero-Garrido, Alexander, et al. 'Quantifying nations' exposure to traffic observation and selective tampering.' PAM 2022. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-98785-5_29
Domestic.Background: The 2/3 threshold is that paper's own choice (Gamero-Garrido, Carisimo, Hao, Huffaker, Snoeren, and Dainotti, PAM 2022, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-98785-5_29, Best Dataset award) for classifying an AS's IP address space as domestic vs. foreign, which the authors then used to study what fraction of a country's transit links come from foreign providers vs. domestic customers -- i.e., a country's exposure to traffic observation by foreign parties. See Appendix H of the AS Tagging paper (Chen, Bischof, Testart, and Dainotti, IMC 2026, https://doi.org/10.1145/3777912.3839831), which also shows how raising the threshold to 90% changes the count of domestic ASes for several countries.
Domestic.Logic: An AS originates at least two-thirds of its IP addresses geolocated in the given country.

Major Access.Description: Major access AS. Defined by Carisimo, Esteban, et al. 'Identifying ASes of state-owned internet operators.' IMC 2021. https://doi.org/10.1145/3487552.3487822
Major Access.Background: The 5% threshold is that paper's own choice (Carisimo, Gamero-Garrido, Snoeren, and Dainotti, IMC 2021, https://doi.org/10.1145/3487552.3487822) for one signal used to identify state-owned Internet operators within a country: an AS is a "major access" network there if it originates more than 5% of the country's globally routed IP address space (summed across geolocation datasets). See Appendix H of the AS Tagging paper (Chen, Bischof, Testart, and Dainotti, IMC 2026, https://doi.org/10.1145/3777912.3839831).
Major Access.Logic: An AS originates more than 5% of the country's globally routed IP addresses.

Global Transit Nth-ranked.Description: Global transit significance ranking using Borda count aggregation over 5 transit metrics.
Global Transit Nth-ranked.Background: Introduced in Appendix G.3 of the AS Tagging paper (Chen, Bischof, Testart, and Dainotti, IMC 2026, https://doi.org/10.1145/3777912.3839831) to rank ASes by overall transit significance without relying on any single metric. The 5 atomic tags and the top_n=50 cutoff are the paper's own choices; Table 6 of the paper shows the resulting ranking reproduces the expected dominance of Tier-1 ASes while also surfacing significant non-Tier-1 transit providers, e.g. AS58453 (China Mobile) and AS4637 (Telstra).
Global Transit Nth-ranked.Logic: Aggregate Borda point rankings from: customer_cnt, cone_/24_cnt, cone_/64_cnt, global_hege_v4, global_hege_v6. Lower rank = more significant.
